Erdős problem #251

The prime-gap dyadic series

Is the dyadic series ∑𝑝𝑛/2𝑛∑pn/2n over consecutive primes irrational? Equivalently, is the corresponding consecutive-prime-gap dyadic series irrational?

Open Problem on GitHub
ResultsPapersLean mapWhat is checked

Results and open questions

#251. A public Lean declaration constructs a synthetic sequence of positive even digits bounded by 4log⁡(𝑛 +1) +244log⁡(n+1)+24. Its dyadic sum is exactly 66, every complete scaled tail and every tail shift is integral, the values 22 and 44 recur arbitrarily late in every residue class, and its increasing odd cumulative positions satisfy 𝑃𝑛/(𝑛log⁡𝑛) →1Pn/(nlog⁡n)→1. The reasoning paper states the combined theorem explicitly. This rules out a much richer package of plausible soft inputs than unboundedness or nonperiodicity alone, but these digits are not the actual prime gaps. The declaration is source-backed and does not yet have a curated claim row.

Independently, a sparse perturbation of the prime gaps can have a rational dyadic sum while retaining the prime growth scale, every fixed eventual congruence, and asymptotically the same short-block statistics. The later positions are not asserted to be prime. This is complementary to Land’s conditional result, not a refutation. Lean checks the finite pair, buffer, and filling identities; the infinite schedule and block-law transfer are ordinary mathematics in the short paper. This obstruction shows that those coarse statistics alone do not force irrationality. The exact prime-gap summation-by-parts equivalence still proves neither the prime-gap series nor the original series irrational; a prime-specific sieve or tail bridge remains open.

Preserving more of the actual gaps.

The quadratic example has the wrong cumulative growth to imitate the primes. A different construction addresses that limitation. If 𝐴 =∑𝑛≥0𝑎𝑛2−(𝑛+1)A=∑n≥0an2−(n+1) converges, fix 𝑀 ≥1M≥1 and a cutoff 𝐾K, and choose a rational 𝑟 ∈(𝐴,𝐴 +𝑀2−𝐾)r∈(A,A+M2−K). Write

2𝐾(𝑟−𝐴)𝑀=∑𝑗≥0𝛿𝑗2𝑗+1,𝛿𝑗∈{0,1}.2K(r−A)M=∑j≥0δj2j+1,δj∈{0,1}.

Set 𝑏𝑛 =𝑎𝑛bn=an for 𝑛 <𝐾n<K and 𝑏𝐾+𝑗 =𝑎𝐾+𝑗 +𝑀𝛿𝑗bK+j=aK+j+Mδj. Then ∑𝑛≥0𝑏𝑛2−(𝑛+1) =𝑟∑n≥0bn2−(n+1)=r. Every coefficient retains its residue modulo 𝑀M and changes by at most 𝑀M; each cumulative sum changes by at most 𝑀𝑛Mn. Applied to prime gaps, this retains the cumulative 𝑛log⁡𝑛nlog⁡n scale. Taking 𝑀M even retains parity as well. Thus a bounded residue-preserving perturbation can have a rational value without sharing the polynomial example’s growth. Neither construction asserts that its cumulative sums are prime.

Sparse corrections and local information.

A single changed coefficient can alter every later cumulative residue. We therefore pair corrections: changing their allocation changes the dyadic value while leaving their unweighted total fixed. Sparsity has a separate job. Most short blocks then meet no correction at all, which preserves their empirical distributions without requiring the corrected positions to be prime.

The reconstructed positions retain their congruences and cumulative growth; they are not asserted to be prime.

The prime series and its tails.

Index the primes from zero: 𝑝0 =2p0=2, 𝑝1 =3p1=3, and 𝑔𝑛 =𝑝𝑛+1 −𝑝𝑛gn=pn+1−pn. In this notation Erdős Problem #251 asks whether

Π=∑𝑛≥0𝑝𝑛2𝑛+1is irrational.Π=∑n≥0pn2n+1is irrational.

This is the usual one-based series 2/2 +3/4 +5/8 +⋯2/2+3/4+5/8+⋯. The first gaps are 11, 22, 2,4,2,4,2,4,6,22,4,2,4,2,4,6,2; only 𝑔0g0 is odd. Let 𝐺 =∑𝑛≥0𝑔𝑛2−(𝑛+1)G=∑n≥0gn2−(n+1). The exact identities are

Π=2+𝐺,𝑇𝑁=∑𝑗≥1𝑔𝑁+𝑗2𝑗,𝑇0=2𝐺−1,𝑇𝑁+1=2𝑇𝑁−𝑔𝑁+1.Π=2+G,TN=∑j≥1gN+j2j,T0=2G−1,TN+1=2TN−gN+1.

Convergence and the identification of these actual tails are established below. They are not additional assumptions under a hypothetical rational value of ΠΠ.

What remains to be distinguished.

For any integer-digit recurrence, iteration gives

𝑇𝑁=2𝑁𝑇0−𝐵𝑁,𝑇𝑁+ℎ−𝑇𝑁=2𝑁(2ℎ−1)𝑇0−𝐶𝑁,ℎ,𝐵𝑁,𝐶𝑁,ℎ∈ℤ.TN=2NT0−BN,TN+h−TN=2N(2h−1)T0−CN,h,BN,CN,h∈Z.

A rational initial value forces an eventual integral shift; an irrational initial value permits no integral positive shift. This is the arithmetic reason for the lcm-diagonal criterion in Theorem 2.1. A more local sufficient condition uses two adjacent shift values in ( −1,1)(−1,1) and a nonzero associated gap difference. If both values were integral they would be zero, contradicting their recurrence. The missing input is their joint occurrence at arbitrarily late indices for every positive shift. The countermodels show why several coarse hypotheses do not supply it.

Relation to prior work.

Erdős stated the fixed-denominator question in his work on irrational series [1] . His irrationality result for prime numerators with factorial denominators does not apply to this dyadic denominator sequence. Kovač’s counterexample to a related variable-denominator expectation likewise does not decide the fixed-denominator problem [16]. An adjacent dyadic theorem of Erdős and Pomerance concerns bounded digits recording comparisons of the largest prime factors of consecutive integers [3]; our prime numerators and gaps are unbounded. Land posted in 2026 a proof of irrationality conditional on Kuperberg’s uniform Hardy-Littlewood prime-tuples conjecture, together with a Lean formalisation of that conditional argument . Nothing in this note is conditional on a prime-tuples hypothesis, and Erdős Problem #251 remains open unconditionally. Interval filling of the kind used in Proposition 1.1 has recent precedents for sums of unit fractions. Kovač and Tao use it to show that bounded perturbations of the denominators 2𝑛2n can give a rational sum, for instance ∑𝑛≥11/(2𝑛 +𝑏𝑛) =3/4∑n≥11/(2n+bn)=3/4 with every 𝑏𝑛 ∈{1,…,5}bn∈{1,…,5}, answering a question of Erdős and Graham on irrationality sequences [7]. Van Doorn and Kovač combine dense filling with a divisibility chain among distinguished terms that eventually absorbs every positive integer, so that finite reciprocal sums take every rational value in an interval [13]. The corrections in Proposition 1.1 use a chain of factorial moduli with the same absorption property to preserve every fixed eventual congruence. The detailed historical comparisons and their hypotheses belong to the companion reasoning record. No priority claim is made for the elementary identities or constructions in this note.

Notation and organisation.

Write ℕ ={0,1,…}N={0,1,…}, ℤZ for the integers, Irr⁡(𝑥)Irr⁡(x) for irrationality, den⁡(𝑞)den⁡(q) for the reduced denominator of 𝑞 ∈ℚq∈Q, and 𝜑φ for Euler’s totient. Section 2 isolates the recurrence-level classifiers and the polynomial obstruction. Section 3 proves the actual prime-to-gap identity; Section 4 proves the shift classification and local criterion. Section 5 explains the remaining carry freedom, and Section 6 states the exact prime-specific obligation. The sources and verification boundary are recorded after the mathematics.

Proof. Substituting 𝐷𝑁+𝑟 =2𝑟𝐷𝑁 −𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟DN+r=2rDN−Bh,N,r into A𝑁,𝑟AN,r cancels the observed block from both sides and leaves 𝐷𝑁 =2𝑧DN=2z. This proves (2.1). After one recurrence step, evenness of 𝛿𝑁δN identifies even integrality at 𝑁 +1N+1 with ordinary integrality at 𝑁N. The forward implication in (2.2) follows, while the reverse implication chooses a nonintegral 𝐷𝑁DN and the legal depth 𝑟 =0r=0.

For (2.4), eventual integrality and the block identity give some 𝑧 ∈ℤz∈Z with

𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟−2𝑟𝑧=−𝐷𝑁+𝑟,Bh,N,r−2rz=−DN+r,

so the displayed strict separation contradicts |𝐷𝑁+𝑟| ≤𝑏(𝑁 +𝑟)|DN+r|≤b(N+r). Conversely, if 𝐷𝑁DN is nonintegral and has reduced denominator 𝑞q, then its distance from every integer is at least 1/𝑞1/q. Choose 𝑟r from (2.3), scale this separation by 2𝑟2r, and use the block identity together with |𝐷𝑁+𝑟| ≤𝑏(𝑁 +𝑟)|DN+r|≤b(N+r). The triangle inequality gives |𝐵ℎ,𝑁,𝑟 −2𝑟𝑧| >𝑏(𝑁 +𝑟)|Bh,N,r−2rz|>b(N+r) for every integer 𝑧z. ◻

The three displayed equivalences are assembled in one declaration, affine circularity bundle.

The first equivalence shows that the apparent affine hierarchy contains no depth-dependent information: it is the pullback of even integrality through the recurrence identity. The fixed lattice removes that data dependence, but under the stated growth condition rational denominator separation already forces every required escape. Hence neither cofinal condition is an independent source of information about consecutive primes.

Finally, the coarse coefficient profile itself has an exact infinite counterexample.

Proposition 2.4 (quadratic polynomial-shift countermodel). Put

𝑎𝑛=2(𝑛2+4𝑛+2),𝑈𝑛=2(𝑛+4)2.an=2(n2+4n+2),Un=2(n+4)2.

The eight displayed clauses are assembled as one statement in polynomial countermodel.

Summation by parts, with the endpoint retained

Summation by parts trades a sequence for its consecutive differences. The form recorded here is exact: it carries no error term, it assumes nothing about the sequence, and it retains the endpoint term rather than absorbing it into an estimate. For a sequence 𝑃P of rational numbers and 𝑛 ≥0n≥0 put

𝐷(𝑃,𝑛)=𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑃(𝑖)2𝑖+1,Δ(𝑃,𝑛)=𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑃(𝑖+1)−𝑃(𝑖)2𝑖+1,D(P,n)=∑i=0n−1P(i)2i+1,Δ(P,n)=∑i=0n−1P(i+1)−P(i)2i+1,

both empty, hence zero, at 𝑛 =0n=0. We call these the dyadic partial sum and the dyadic difference sum of 𝑃P.

Proposition 3.1 (finite summation by parts). For every rational sequence 𝑃P and every 𝑛 ≥0n≥0,

𝐷(𝑃,𝑛+1)=𝑃(0)+Δ(𝑃,𝑛)−𝑃(𝑛)2𝑛+1.D(P,n+1)=P(0)+Δ(P,n)−P(n)2n+1.

Proof. Expand the difference sum and shift its first index. All interior coefficients of 𝑃(𝑖)P(i) become 2−𝑖−12−i−1; the remaining terms are 𝑃(0)P(0) and the displayed endpoint −𝑃(𝑛)2−𝑛−1−P(n)2−n−1. This also covers 𝑛 =0n=0. ◻

This is the finite summation by parts. No positivity, monotonicity or convergence is required.

Specialising to 𝑃(𝑖) =𝑝𝑖P(i)=pi, whose first value is 𝑝0 =2p0=2, and writing 𝑔𝑖 =𝑝𝑖+1 −𝑝𝑖gi=pi+1−pi for the zero-based gaps, gives the reformulation. The displayed partial sums with denominators 2𝑖2i are twice these, by the factor-of-two identity.

Theorem 3.2 (prime-gap reformulation). Let 𝑝0 =2,𝑝1 =3,…p0=2,p1=3,… be the primes in increasing order and 𝑔𝑖 =𝑝𝑖+1 −𝑝𝑖gi=pi+1−pi. For every 𝑛 ≥0n≥0,

𝑛∑𝑖=0𝑝𝑖2𝑖+1=2+𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝑔𝑖2𝑖+1−𝑝𝑛2𝑛+1.∑i=0npi2i+1=2+∑i=0n−1gi2i+1−pn2n+1.

This is the prime-gap summation by parts. The leading 22 is 𝑝0p0. At 𝑛 =2n=2 both sides equal 19/819/8. The identity is the already-known summation-by-parts (Tao on the erdosproblems.com/251 thread, 7 October 2025); this checkout checks it and does not claim priority.

The infinite identity and the irrationality equivalence

Write

𝑢𝑛=𝑝𝑛2𝑛+1,𝑣𝑛=𝑔𝑛2𝑛+1un=pn2n+1,vn=gn2n+1

for the prime dyadic terms and the prime-gap dyadic terms, so that ∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛 =Π∑n≥0un=Π. The termwise identity 𝑣𝑛 =2𝑢𝑛+1 −𝑢𝑛vn=2un+1−un is the dyadic discrete derivative. It expresses each gap term as an integer combination of two consecutive prime terms, so once (𝑢𝑛)(un) is summable the gap series can be summed by rearranging two copies of the prime series, which is what the following proof does.

Theorem 3.3 (infinite prime-gap identity). Let 𝑢𝑛 =𝑝𝑛/2𝑛+1un=pn/2n+1 and 𝑣𝑛 =𝑔𝑛/2𝑛+1vn=gn/2n+1. If (𝑢𝑛)(un) is summable, then (𝑣𝑛)(vn) is summable and

∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛=2+∑𝑛≥0𝑣𝑛.∑n≥0un=2+∑n≥0vn.

Proof. The shifted sequence (𝑢𝑛+1)(un+1) is summable. Sum 𝑣𝑛 =2𝑢𝑛+1 −𝑢𝑛vn=2un+1−un and use 𝑢0 =1u0=1:

∑𝑛≥0𝑣𝑛=2(∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛−𝑢0)−∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛=∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛−2.∑n≥0vn=2(∑n≥0un−u0)−∑n≥0un=∑n≥0un−2.

◻

The summability transfer is the gap-series summability theorem, and the displayed identity is the infinite prime-gap identity. Summability of both series is part of the conclusion in infinite prime gap identity rather than a hypothesis carried by the reader.

Corollary 3.4 (exact irrationality reformulation). With 𝑢𝑛un and 𝑣𝑛vn as in Theorem 3.3, and (𝑢𝑛)(un) summable,

Irr(∑𝑛≥0𝑢𝑛)⟺Irr(∑𝑛≥0𝑣𝑛).Irr(∑n≥0un)⟺Irr(∑n≥0vn).

The corresponding zero-based series with denominator 2𝑛2n is 4 +2∑𝑛≥0𝑣𝑛4+2∑n≥0vn and has the same irrationality status. Termwise it is twice the normalised series, by the infinite factor-of-two identity.

These are the normalised irrationality equivalence, the displayed-series identity, and the displayed-series irrationality equivalence. The three clauses are also available as the single declaration irrationality reformulation.

The summability hypothesis.

The formal source now proves the elementary polynomial bound 𝑝𝑛 ≤1250(𝑛 +1)4pn≤1250(n+1)4, using prime counting and central-binomial growth, and deduces summability directly (polynomial bound, summability). Thus Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 3.4 are now unconditional. The unconditional infinite prime-gap identity removes the summability hypothesis; the prime number theorem remains useful context but is no longer a proof dependency of this note. The open content is exactly irrationality of the prime-gap series. Concretely, Π =3.674643966…Π=3.674643966… is irrational if and only if ∑𝑛≥0𝑔𝑛2−(𝑛+1) =1.674643966…∑n≥0gn2−(n+1)=1.674643966… is, and neither is known.

The tail recurrence and integral shifts

The series is not attacked directly. Suppose ∑𝑖≥0𝑎𝑖2−(𝑖+1)∑i≥0ai2−(i+1) converges, with every 𝑎𝑖ai an integer, and rescale its tails by putting

𝑇𝑁=2𝑁+1∑𝑖>𝑁𝑎𝑖2𝑖+1=∑𝑗≥1𝑎𝑁+𝑗2𝑗.TN=2N+1∑i>Nai2i+1=∑j≥1aN+j2j.

Two facts follow immediately. First 𝑇𝑁+1 =2𝑇𝑁 −𝑎𝑁+1TN+1=2TN−aN+1, so moving one level along doubles the rescaled tail and subtracts a single coefficient. Second 𝑇0 =2∑𝑖≥0𝑎𝑖2−(𝑖+1) −𝑎0T0=2∑i≥0ai2−(i+1)−a0, so the sum is rational exactly when 𝑇0T0 is. The whole of Section 4 therefore studies that recurrence in isolation, assuming nothing about the coefficients beyond the fact that they are integers; the prime-gap instance is resumed at the end of the section. The following definition is the object so obtained, stripped of its origin.

Definition 4.1. Let 𝑔 :ℕ →ℤg:N→Z and 𝑇 :ℕ →ℚT:N→Q. Say 𝑇T satisfies the dyadic tail recurrence with digits 𝑔g when

𝑇𝑁+1=2𝑇𝑁−𝑔𝑁+1for every 𝑁.TN+1=2TN−gN+1for every N.

We call the sequence (𝑇𝑁)𝑁≥0(TN)N≥0 the orbit of 𝑇0T0 under 𝑔g, write 𝜎ℎ(𝑁) =𝑇𝑁+ℎ −𝑇𝑁σh(N)=TN+h−TN for the shift of length ℎh at 𝑁N, and call a rational number integral when it is the image of an integer.

These are the tail recurrence, the shift, and integrality. The digits are arbitrary integers. In the intended instance they are the prime gaps and 𝑇𝑁TN is the complete gap tail ∑𝑗≥1𝑔𝑁+𝑗2−𝑗∑j≥1gN+j2−j. That identification, and the recurrence over ℝR with no rationality hypothesis, already sit in RealPrimeGapTail.lean. Every statement below is a theorem about Definition 4.1.

One small orbit, referred to again below, is worth having in view. Take every digit 𝑔𝑁 =0gN=0 and 𝑇0 =1/12T0=1/12. Then 𝑇𝑁+1 =2𝑇𝑁TN+1=2TN, so the orbit is 112,16,13,23,43,…112,16,13,23,43,…, and 𝜎ℎ(𝑁) =(2ℎ −1)2𝑁/12σh(N)=(2h−1)2N/12. The shift of length 22 is not integral at 𝑁 =0N=0, where 𝜎2(0) =13 −112 =14σ2(0)=13−112=14, and is integral at 𝑁 =2N=2, where 𝜎2(2) =43 −13 =1σ2(2)=43−13=1; the shift of length 11 is 𝜎1(𝑁) =2𝑁/12σ1(N)=2N/12 and is never integral. The change at 𝑁 =2N=2 is accounted for by Theorem 4.6, and the failure at ℎ =1h=1 by Theorem 4.3.

Iterating the recurrence ℎh times multiplies 𝑇𝑁TN by 2ℎ2h and accumulates an explicit integer, which we now name. Define 𝐵0,𝑁 =0B0,N=0 and 𝐵ℎ+1,𝑁 =2𝐵ℎ,𝑁 +𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1Bh+1,N=2Bh,N+gN+h+1, so that 𝐵ℎ,𝑁 =𝑔𝑁+12ℎ−1 +⋯ +𝑔𝑁+ℎBh,N=gN+12h−1+⋯+gN+h: the tail block. Thus 𝐵1,𝑁 =𝑔𝑁+1B1,N=gN+1, 𝐵2,𝑁 =2𝑔𝑁+1 +𝑔𝑁+2B2,N=2gN+1+gN+2 and 𝐵3,𝑁 =4𝑔𝑁+1 +2𝑔𝑁+2 +𝑔𝑁+3B3,N=4gN+1+2gN+2+gN+3: the block puts the weights 2ℎ−1,…,202h−1,…,20 on the ℎh digits following index 𝑁N.

Theorem 4.2 (block identity). Let 𝑇 :ℕ →ℚT:N→Q satisfy the dyadic tail recurrence with integer digits 𝑔g, and let 𝐵ℎ,𝑁Bh,N be as above. For every 𝑁N and ℎh,

𝑇𝑁+ℎ=2ℎ𝑇𝑁−𝐵ℎ,𝑁,hence𝜎ℎ(𝑁)=(2ℎ−1)𝑇𝑁−𝐵ℎ,𝑁.TN+h=2hTN−Bh,N,henceσh(N)=(2h−1)TN−Bh,N.

Proof. Induct on ℎh using the recursions for 𝑇T and 𝐵B, then subtract 𝑇𝑁TN to obtain the shift identity. ◻

The first identity is the iterated block identity; the second is the scaled shift identity. Both are also assembled in block identity, and the real-state form is real block identity.

The shifts themselves satisfy the shift step identity

𝜎ℎ(𝑁+1)=2𝜎ℎ(𝑁)−(𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1−𝑔𝑁+1).σh(N+1)=2σh(N)−(gN+h+1−gN+1).

Since 𝐵ℎ,𝑁Bh,N is an integer, Theorem 4.2 converts a question about the shift into a question about the single scaled term (2ℎ −1)𝑇𝑁(2h−1)TN.

Theorem 4.3 (integral-shift criterion). Let 𝑇 :ℕ →ℚT:N→Q satisfy the dyadic tail recurrence with integer digits 𝑔g. For every 𝑁N and ℎh, the shift 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) is integral if and only if (2ℎ −1)𝑇𝑁(2h−1)TN is integral.

Proof. By Theorem 4.2 the two differ by the integer 𝐵ℎ,𝑁Bh,N, and subtracting an integer does not change integrality, by the integer-shift invariance. ◻

This is the integral-shift criterion. Thus integrality depends only on the reduced denominator of 𝑇𝑁TN.

The denominator criterion is exact:

𝜎ℎ(𝑁)∈ℤ⟺den⁡(𝑇𝑁)∣2ℎ−1.(3.4)(3.4)σh(N)∈Z⟺den⁡(TN)∣2h−1.

This is the denominator classification. Euler’s totient supplies one admissible shift length when the denominator is odd; it is a witness, not the classification itself.

Theorem 4.4 (a shift of totient length). Let 𝑇 :ℕ →ℚT:N→Q satisfy the dyadic tail recurrence with integer digits 𝑔g, and let 𝜑φ be Euler’s totient function. If the reduced denominator 𝑑d of 𝑇𝑁TN is odd, then 𝜎𝜑(𝑑)(𝑁)σφ(d)(N) is integral.

Proof. Since 𝑑d is odd, 22 and 𝑑d are coprime, so Euler’s congruence gives 2𝜑(𝑑) ≡1(mod𝑑)2φ(d)≡1(modd), that is 𝑑 ∣2𝜑(𝑑) −1d∣2φ(d)−1. Writing 2𝜑(𝑑) −1 =𝑑𝑘2φ(d)−1=dk and 𝑇𝑁 =𝑢/𝑑TN=u/d in lowest terms, (2𝜑(𝑑) −1)𝑇𝑁 =𝑘𝑢(2φ(d)−1)TN=ku is an integer, and Theorem 4.3 transfers this to the shift. The Euler multiplier itself is the totient multiplier at odd denominator. ◻

This is the totient shift.

For den⁡𝑇𝑁 =3den⁡TN=3, the shift of length 22 is integral while the shift of length 11 is not. For denominator 55, length 44 is admissible.

The hypothesis is a genuine restriction: the argument uses coprimality of 22 with the denominator, and the even part of a denominator is exactly what the doubling in the recurrence acts on. It cannot be dropped. If 𝑇𝑁 =1/2TN=1/2 then 2ℎ −12h−1 is odd for every ℎ ≥1h≥1, so (2ℎ −1)𝑇𝑁(2h−1)TN is never an integer and, by Theorem 4.3, no shift at 𝑁N is integral.

Theorem 4.5 (propagation). Let 𝑇 :ℕ →ℚT:N→Q satisfy the dyadic tail recurrence with integer digits 𝑔g, and fix ℎh and 𝑁N. If 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) is integral, then 𝜎ℎ(𝑁 +𝑘)σh(N+k) is integral for every 𝑘 ≥0k≥0.

Proof. By the shift step identity, 𝜎ℎ(𝑁 +1) =2𝜎ℎ(𝑁) −(𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 −𝑔𝑁+1)σh(N+1)=2σh(N)−(gN+h+1−gN+1) is an integer combination of an integer and two digits; this is the one-step propagation, and the claim follows by induction on 𝑘k. ◻

This is the propagation to every later index.

The three preceding theorems combine as follows, and this is the statement the rest of the note rests on. The special case is immediate: if den⁡𝑇0den⁡T0 is already odd, then Theorem 4.4 at 𝑁 =0N=0 makes the shift of length 𝜑(den⁡𝑇0)φ(den⁡T0) integral and Theorem 4.5 keeps it integral at every later index, so one may take 𝑁0 =0N0=0. In general a denominator carries a power of two as well, and the key point is that the doubling in the recurrence annihilates exactly the 22-adic part of a denominator, and nothing else: after finitely many steps the orbit therefore reaches a term with odd reduced denominator, which is precisely the situation Theorem 4.4 handles. No control of the digits is needed anywhere.

Theorem 4.6 (exact denominator dynamics and eventual integrality). Let 𝑇 :ℕ →ℚT:N→Q satisfy the dyadic tail recurrence with integer digits 𝑔g (Definition 4.1). Then some fixed positive shift is integral from some point onwards:

∃ℎ≥1 ∃𝑁0 ∀𝑁≥𝑁0,𝜎ℎ(𝑁)∈ℤ.∃h≥1 ∃N0 ∀N≥N0,σh(N)∈Z.

Proof. At every step the reduced denominator obeys the exact recurrence

den⁡(𝑇𝑁+1)=den⁡(𝑇𝑁)gcd(2,den⁡(𝑇𝑁)).den⁡(TN+1)=den⁡(TN)gcd(2,den⁡(TN)).

Thus each even denominator loses exactly one factor of 22, while an odd denominator is unchanged. After finitely many steps the denominator is odd. Theorem 4.4, applied at that index 𝑠s, supplies the positive shift ℎ =𝜑(den⁡𝑇𝑠)h=φ(den⁡Ts), and Theorem 4.5 keeps that shift integral at every later index. ◻

The one-step formula is the denominator recurrence, with its odd case and even case.

In the orbit displayed after Definition 4.1 the proof runs as follows: den⁡𝑇0 =12 =22 ⋅3den⁡T0=12=22⋅3, so 𝑠 =2s=2, the orbit reaches 𝑇2 =1/3T2=1/3 with odd denominator, and ℎ =𝜑(3) =2h=φ(3)=2. That is exactly the shift length seen to be integral there from index 22 onwards, and no shorter one works.

Three features of the argument are used later. The proof may take as its number of preparatory steps the 22-adic valuation of den⁡𝑇0den⁡T0. The resulting shift length ℎh is the totient of the odd denominator reached from a hypothetical rational initial value, and is not known in advance for the prime-gap orbit. This is why this argument requires Problem 6.2 for every ℎh, rather than for one preassigned shift length. Finally, the digits enter only through the integer 𝐵𝑠,0Bs,0, so the conclusion holds for an arbitrary integer digit sequence.

Denominator factorisation and cancellation are the power-of-two/odd denominator scaling and the multiplier at the two-adic exponent, packaged in the fixed-denominator theorem; the quantified conclusion is the eventual integral-shift theorem for the actual prime-gap tail state. The displayed indexed form is eventual integral positive shift.

The useful contrapositive is stated for a real recurrence. Call its shifts cofinally non-integral when, for every fixed ℎ ≥1h≥1 and every threshold 𝑁0N0, some 𝑁 ≥𝑁0N≥N0 has 𝜎ℎ(𝑁) ∉ℤσh(N)∉Z. This is precisely the negation of the conclusion of Theorem 4.6: no shift length whatever becomes integral and stays integral.

Theorem 4.7 (exact rationality classification). Let 𝑇 :ℕ →ℝT:N→R satisfy 𝑇𝑁+1 =2𝑇𝑁 −𝑔𝑁+1TN+1=2TN−gN+1 with integer 𝑔g. If its shifts are defined by 𝜎ℎ(𝑁) =𝑇𝑁+ℎ −𝑇𝑁σh(N)=TN+h−TN, then the following are equivalent:

  1. 𝑇0T0 is rational;

  2. 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) is integral for some ℎ ≥1h≥1 and some 𝑁N;

  3. for some fixed ℎ ≥1h≥1, 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) is integral at every sufficiently large 𝑁N.

Consequently 𝑇0T0 is irrational if and only if every positive-length shift is non-integral at every index, equivalently if and only if the shifts are cofinally non-integral.

Proof. For (i)⇒⇒(iii), choose 𝑞 ∈ℚq∈Q whose real cast is 𝑇0T0. The real block identity identifies the whole orbit with the cast of the rational recurrence starting at 𝑞q; Theorem 4.6 applied to that rational orbit then gives (iii). The implication (iii)⇒⇒(ii) is immediate. For (ii)⇒⇒(i), the real block identity gives

𝜎ℎ(𝑁)=(2ℎ−1)𝑇𝑁−𝐵ℎ,𝑁.σh(N)=(2h−1)TN−Bh,N.

Here 𝐵ℎ,𝑁Bh,N and 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) are integers and 2ℎ −1 ≠02h−1≠0, so 𝑇𝑁TN is rational. Iterating the recurrence backwards through the block identity then makes 𝑇0T0 rational. Negating the pointwise and eventual forms gives the two irrationality formulations. ◻

The rational actual-tail state obeys the tail recurrence, and a hypothetical rational value of the gap series supplies the rational-tail representation. The exact real classifiers are one integral positive shift, eventual integrality, pointwise non-integrality, and cofinal non-integrality. All four equivalences are collected in rationality classification.

The actual prime-gap orbit.

The concrete tails

𝑇𝑁=∑𝑗≥1𝑔𝑁+𝑗2𝑗TN=∑j≥1gN+j2j

are already identified, with no rationality hypothesis. The polynomial prime bound gives convergence, and 𝑇𝑁+1 =2𝑇𝑁 −𝑔𝑁+1TN+1=2TN−gN+1 is the same identification. If 𝐺 =∑𝑛≥0𝑔𝑛/2𝑛+1G=∑n≥0gn/2n+1, then 𝑇0 =2𝐺 −1T0=2G−1. Together with Theorem 3.3, this shows that ΠΠ, 𝐺G, and 𝑇0T0 have the same rationality status. Thus Theorem 4.7 identifies Problem #251 exactly with cofinal shift escape for 𝑇T. The older rational-candidate representation remains in PrimeGapDyadicTail.lean. What is not proved is the cofinal non-integrality needed by Theorem 4.7.

Two adjacent small shifts cannot both be integral

The exact classifier reduces irrationality to cofinal non-integrality, a condition of infinite precision imposed on a complete tail. The key point is that inside the open interval ( −1,1)(−1,1) integrality is equality with zero, so on that range the one-step shift recurrence

𝜎ℎ(𝑁+1)=2𝜎ℎ(𝑁)−(𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1−𝑔𝑁+1)σh(N+1)=2σh(N)−(gN+h+1−gN+1)

turns simultaneous integrality of two adjacent shifts into a single comparison of digits. What this buys is a certificate: a condition attached to a single pair of adjacent indices, whose verification already contradicts integrality at that pair. The point of arranging the argument this way is that the distance of a shift from the integers never has to be estimated; it suffices to know that both shifts lie in ( −1,1)(−1,1) and that two digits differ.

Theorem 4.8 (adjacent small-shift obstruction). Let 𝑇 :ℕ →ℚT:N→Q satisfy the dyadic tail recurrence with integer digits 𝑔g. Fix ℎh and 𝑁N. If

−1<𝜎ℎ(𝑁)<1,−1<𝜎ℎ(𝑁+1)<1,𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1≠𝑔𝑁+1,−1<σh(N)<1,−1<σh(N+1)<1,gN+h+1≠gN+1,

then 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) and 𝜎ℎ(𝑁 +1)σh(N+1) cannot both be integral. Consequently, if such a pair occurs beyond every threshold, the ℎh-shift is not eventually integral.

Proof. An integral rational strictly between −1−1 and 11 is zero. If both shifts were integral, both would therefore vanish, and substitution in the displayed shift step identity would give 𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 =𝑔𝑁+1gN+h+1=gN+1, a contradiction. The cofinal statement chooses one such adjacent pair after the alleged onset of integrality. ◻

The finite contradiction is the adjacent small-shift obstruction; its quantified form is the cofinal small-mismatch theorem; and the actual-prime-gap specialisation is the prime-gap specialisation. Theorem 4.8 is conditional on its two tail inequalities; no theorem asserting that such pairs occur is claimed here. The local obstruction and its cofinal consequence are stated as one declaration in rational small pair bundle.

All three are stated for a rational orbit, while the prime-gap tail 𝑇T of Section 4 is real, so the rational statement does not on its own discharge the instances that arise downstream. The same argument gives the real form directly.

Corollary 4.9 (adjacent small-shift obstruction, real form). Let 𝑇 :ℕ →ℝT:N→R satisfy 𝑇𝑁+1 =2𝑇𝑁 −𝑔𝑁+1TN+1=2TN−gN+1 with integer digits 𝑔g, and write 𝜎ℎ(𝑁) =𝑇𝑁+ℎ −𝑇𝑁σh(N)=TN+h−TN. Fix ℎh and 𝑁N. If

−1<𝜎ℎ(𝑁)<1,−1<𝜎ℎ(𝑁+1)<1,𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1≠𝑔𝑁+1,−1<σh(N)<1,−1<σh(N+1)<1,gN+h+1≠gN+1,

then 𝜎ℎ(𝑁)σh(N) and 𝜎ℎ(𝑁 +1)σh(N+1) do not both lie in ℤZ. Consequently, if such a pair occurs beyond every threshold, the ℎh-shift is not eventually integral.

Proof. The shift identity holds over ℝR, and the only integer in ( −1,1)(−1,1) is still zero. Thus the proof of Theorem 4.8 applies without change, including its cofinal conclusion. ◻

Corollary 4.9 is real small pair bundle, and the resulting implication for the actual prime series is real small pair prime endpoint. These live declarations can postdate the historical public snapshot used by the source links.

The third hypothesis, on its own, is available. For the actual gaps tabulated in Section 1 it reads 𝑔4 =2 ≠4 =𝑔3g4=2≠4=g3 at ℎ =1h=1, 𝑁 =2N=2; and Proposition 4.10 below says precisely that for each fixed ℎ ≥1h≥1 the inequality 𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 ≠𝑔𝑁+1gN+h+1≠gN+1 holds for arbitrarily large 𝑁N, since its failure from some index onwards is eventual periodicity with period ℎh. What is missing is their joint occurrence with the digit mismatch at the same indices. Each inequality constrains a complete infinite tail.

Proposition 4.10 (prime gaps do not become periodic). For every positive ℎh, the actual consecutive-prime-gap sequence is not eventually periodic with period ℎh.

Proof. The gaps are unbounded, by the standard construction: the interval from 𝑛! +2n!+2 to 𝑛! +𝑛n!+n contains no prime. Far stronger lower bounds for large gaps are known [6], but unboundedness is all that is needed. An eventually periodic natural-valued sequence has finite range after its preperiod, while its finite initial segment is bounded as well; hence it is bounded, a contradiction. ◻

This is the unboundedness of the actual gaps and the non-eventual periodicity of the gap sequence. The statement at the index convention displayed above is prime gaps not eventually periodic. Combining nonperiodicity with eventual strict smallness of one positive shift would also exclude eventual integrality, but eventual smallness at every sufficiently large index is stronger than the cofinal adjacent-pair hypothesis in Theorem 4.8 and is not asserted here.

Nonperiodic coefficients with a rational sum

There is an exact finite obstruction recorded in the pinned source: a second example has finite sum −𝑛/2𝑛−n/2n and non-eventually-periodic coefficients (finite endpoint; coefficient nonperiodicity). The actual prime gaps are also not eventually periodic (prime-gap nonperiodicity), but that fact alone is insufficient.

For a bounded canonical base-two digit expansion, rationality forces eventual periodicity. Prime gaps are unbounded coefficients, so that criterion does not apply. The following telescoping construction shows explicitly how nonperiodic coefficients can have a rational sum.

The construction runs the emission of coefficients backwards. Let 𝐾 :ℕ →ℚK:N→Q be arbitrary, read 𝐾𝑛Kn as the value carried into level 𝑛n, and put 𝜅𝑛 =2𝐾𝑛 −𝐾𝑛+1κn=2Kn−Kn+1: the carry coefficient. That definition is exactly the statement that

𝐾𝑛2𝑛=𝜅𝑛2𝑛+1+𝐾𝑛+12𝑛+1,Kn2n=κn2n+1+Kn+12n+1,

so at each level the carried value splits into one emitted coefficient and a new carry. Nothing at all is assumed about 𝐾K: not integrality, not positivity, not any bound. That is the sense in which the carry is free, and it is what the counterexample below exploits.

Proposition 5.1 (exact telescoping). Let 𝐾 :ℕ →ℚK:N→Q be arbitrary and 𝜅𝑛 =2𝐾𝑛 −𝐾𝑛+1κn=2Kn−Kn+1. For every 𝑛 ≥0n≥0,

𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝜅𝑖2𝑖+1=𝐾0−𝐾𝑛2𝑛.∑i=0n−1κi2i+1=K0−Kn2n.

Proof. A routine induction on 𝑛n; the added term is (2𝐾𝑛 −𝐾𝑛+1)/2𝑛+1 =𝐾𝑛/2𝑛 −𝐾𝑛+1/2𝑛+1(2Kn−Kn+1)/2n+1=Kn/2n−Kn+1/2n+1. ◻

This is the carry telescoping identity.

Consequence for the coefficients.

If 𝐾𝑛2−𝑛 →0Kn2−n→0, the emitted partial sums converge to 𝐾0K0. A parity-compatible positive example is

𝐾0=52,𝐾𝑛=2𝑛+2 (𝑛≥1),𝜅0=1,𝜅𝑛=2𝑛 (𝑛≥1),K0=52,Kn=2n+2 (n≥1),κ0=1,κn=2n (n≥1),

for which

𝑛−1∑𝑖=0𝜅𝑖2𝑖+1=52−𝐾𝑛2𝑛⟶52.∑i=0n−1κi2i+1=52−Kn2n⟶52.

Thus the emitted coefficients 1,2,4,6,8,10,…1,2,4,6,8,10,… are positive, even after the first term, unbounded and not eventually periodic, although their dyadic sum is rational. Rationality alone therefore cannot imply eventual periodicity even for a positive, parity-correct integer coefficient sequence. The example does not claim that these coefficients are prime gaps; it isolates the additional arithmetic information any successful argument must use.

Complements and further questions

Problem #251 is open. Unconditional convergence of both dyadic series, the unconditional infinite prime-gap identity, and the real-to-rational scaled-tail representation are proved. Every rational candidate supplies one positive fixed shift which is integral at every sufficiently late tail index: the eventual integral-shift theorem. The denominator construction selects that same shift so that prime-gap nonperiodicity also rules out its eventual confinement to the open unit interval (not eventually small). This conclusion is compatible with rationality: it says that the rationally forced shift cannot support an eventual-smallness contradiction. It supplies neither eventual smallness nor cofinally many adjacent small mismatches for that shift. The remaining issue is recurrence or anti-concentration of the actual prime-gap shifts. Throughout, 𝑔𝑖 =𝑝𝑖+1 −𝑝𝑖gi=pi+1−pi are the zero-based prime gaps of Section 1. Write 𝖤(ℎ)E(h) for the cofinal escape statement in (5.1) at shift ℎh.

Problem 6.1 (divisor-hitting shift escape). For every 𝑟 ≥1r≥1, does some positive multiple of 𝑟r escape cofinally?

∀𝑟≥1 ∃𝑚≥1:𝖤(𝑚𝑟).∀r≥1 ∃m≥1:E(mr).

Divisor-hitting escape changes the organisation of the quantifiers. Within an integer-digit recurrence it is equivalent to irrationality, just as universal shift escape is: a rational state has a positive eventual order, and every positive multiple of that order is an integral shift. A quantitatively stated sufficient estimate can still be easier to attack, but that requires a separately proved analytic bound. Forward propagation is Theorem 4.5.

Problem 6.2 (universal prime-gap shift escape). For every ℎ ≥1h≥1 and every 𝑁0N0, prove that some 𝑁 ≥𝑁0N≥N0 satisfies

∑𝑗≥1𝑔𝑁+ℎ+𝑗−𝑔𝑁+𝑗2𝑗∉ℤ.(5.1)(5.1)∑j≥1gN+h+j−gN+j2j∉Z.

The series in (5.1) is exactly 𝑇𝑁+ℎ −𝑇𝑁TN+h−TN. Theorem 4.7 makes Problem 6.2 equivalent to irrationality of ΠΠ. Within the integer-digit recurrence, divisor-hitting and universal escape are equivalent: a hypothetical rational value chooses a shift length from the odd part of its reduced denominator, and the cocycle then makes every positive multiple eventually integral. The two formulations organise the quantifiers differently; they do not give a strict logical weakening.

Problem 6.3 (cofinal adjacent small mismatch). For every fixed ℎ ≥1h≥1 and every 𝑁0N0, prove that some 𝑁 ≥𝑁0N≥N0 satisfies

| | | | |∑𝑗≥1𝑔𝑁+ℎ+𝑗−𝑔𝑁+𝑗2𝑗| | | | |<1,| | | | |∑𝑗≥1𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1+𝑗−𝑔𝑁+1+𝑗2𝑗| | | | |<1,𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1≠𝑔𝑁+1.(5.2)(5.2)|∑j≥1gN+h+j−gN+j2j|<1,|∑j≥1gN+h+1+j−gN+1+j2j|<1,gN+h+1≠gN+1.

The two sums are adjacent ℎh-shifts. Corollary 4.9 turns each instance of (5.2) into a finite contradiction to simultaneous integrality; Theorem 4.8 is the rational case. A cofinal family of such pairs therefore proves Problem 6.2; Theorem 4.7 then gives irrationality of the gap series, and Corollary 3.4 transfers it to ΠΠ. The endpoint takes every positive ℎh: a proof only at ℎ =1h=1 eliminates one eventual-integrality possibility and does not discharge the classifier. Digit mismatches and small shifts must occur at the same indices; separate cofinal occurrence statements do not establish that intersection. This formulation deliberately asks only for sporadic adjacent pairs; the stronger assertion that a fixed shift is eventually always smaller than one is unnecessary. The conjunction may have density zero: that excludes a positive-proportion lower bound, but an averaging argument may still produce an unbounded sparse count.

Several natural prime-distribution inputs are insufficient. Isolated small gaps, isolated large gaps, average gap estimates, and the occurrence of any one fixed finite pattern do not suffice: both inequalities in (5.2) contain the complete infinite continuation. Nor does parity: after the first gap all 𝑔𝑛gn are even. Unboundedness and non-eventual-periodicity of the actual gaps, though now checked, do not imply the required small-tail recurrence. In particular, Section 5 shows that no argument can deduce eventual periodicity from rationality alone.

A finite truncation criterion.

Both problems above are stated in terms of infinite tails, but a dominated truncation reduces the first of them to a finite quantity. For 𝐿 ≥1L≥1 put

𝑆ℎ,𝑁,𝐿=𝐿∑𝑗=1𝑔𝑁+ℎ+𝑗−𝑔𝑁+𝑗2𝑗,Sh,N,L=∑j=1LgN+h+j−gN+j2j,

the truncation of the series in (5.1) after 𝐿L terms. This is a finite sum of gap differences and can be computed; the point of the following proposition is to say how far from an integer it must be before the discarded tail is irrelevant.

Equivalently, introduce the integral dyadic block

𝐷ℎ,𝑁,𝐿=𝐿∑𝑗=12𝐿−𝑗(𝑔𝑁+ℎ+𝑗−𝑔𝑁+𝑗),𝑆ℎ,𝑁,𝐿=𝐷ℎ,𝑁,𝐿2𝐿.Dh,N,L=∑j=1L2L−j(gN+h+j−gN+j),Sh,N,L=Dh,N,L2L.

Then

dist⁡(𝑆ℎ,𝑁,𝐿,ℤ)=2−𝐿min{𝐷ℎ,𝑁,𝐿mod2𝐿,2𝐿−(𝐷ℎ,𝑁,𝐿mod2𝐿)}.dist⁡(Sh,N,L,Z)=2−Lmin{Dh,N,Lmod2L,2L−(Dh,N,Lmod2L)}.

Here 𝐷ℎ,𝑁,𝐿mod2𝐿Dh,N,Lmod2L denotes the least nonnegative residue, including when 𝐷ℎ,𝑁,𝐿 <0Dh,N,L<0. Thus the finite criterion below is an exact modular small-arc problem: the residue of 𝐷ℎ,𝑁,𝐿Dh,N,L must avoid the two arcs of radius 2𝐿𝑅ℎ,𝑁,𝐿(𝑀)2LRh,N,L(M) around 00 modulo 2𝐿2L. A one-block certificate would be a prime-gap theorem producing such an avoided arc on a logarithmic block.

Proposition 6.4 (finite truncation). Let 𝑀(𝑛) ≥𝑔𝑛M(n)≥gn for every 𝑛n, assume that the series below converges, and put

𝑅ℎ,𝑁,𝐿(𝑀)=∑𝑗>𝐿𝑀(𝑁+ℎ+𝑗)+𝑀(𝑁+𝑗)2𝑗.Rh,N,L(M)=∑j>LM(N+h+j)+M(N+j)2j.

Suppose that for every fixed ℎ ≥1h≥1 and every 𝑁0N0 there exist 𝑁 ≥𝑁0N≥N0 and 𝐿 ≥1L≥1 with

dist⁡(𝑆ℎ,𝑁,𝐿,ℤ)>𝑅ℎ,𝑁,𝐿(𝑀).(5.3)(5.3)dist⁡(Sh,N,L,Z)>Rh,N,L(M).

Then Problem 6.2 holds.

Proof. The part of ∑𝑗≥1(𝑔𝑁+ℎ+𝑗 −𝑔𝑁+𝑗)2−𝑗∑j≥1(gN+h+j−gN+j)2−j omitted from 𝑆ℎ,𝑁,𝐿Sh,N,L has absolute value at most 𝑅ℎ,𝑁,𝐿(𝑀)Rh,N,L(M), so under eq:truncation the full sum lies at positive distance from every integer. ◻

The last distance-to-integers inference is the elementary paper argument in the displayed proof: an error at most 𝑅R cannot reach an integer when the approximation is farther than 𝑅R from every integer. It is not real integral of error bound, and the proposition itself is cofinal escape of finite truncation. For instance, if 𝑆ℎ,𝑁,𝐿 =3/8Sh,N,L=3/8 and 𝑅ℎ,𝑁,𝐿(𝑀) =1/32Rh,N,L(M)=1/32, the full sum lies within 1/321/32 of 3/83/8 and so at distance at least 11/3211/32 from every integer, which settles (5.1) at that 𝑁N. The prime-gap tail bound, the convergence used above, and the existence of blocks satisfying eq:truncation are not consequences of that inference. The proposition’s full sum is real-valued, and the formal declaration is stated for the real tail throughout. Its conditional endpoint for the actual prime series is irrational prime series of finite truncation.

Taking the classical bound 𝑀(𝑛) ≪𝑛log⁡𝑛M(n)≪nlog⁡n, a choice 𝐿 =⌈𝐴log2⁡(𝑁 +ℎ +2)⌉L=⌈Alog2⁡(N+h+2)⌉ with any fixed 𝐴 >1A>1 makes the right side a negative power of 𝑁N up to logarithms. Thus eq:truncation asks for a finite dyadic anti-concentration estimate on a logarithmic-length block, not control of an infinite tail and not eventual periodicity of the full gap sequence. For Problem 6.3, the same truncation must certify two adjacent full-tail values inside the open unit interval, together with the displayed gap mismatch. A finite prefix is useful only when its omitted tail is rigorously dominated.

What eq:truncation requires is joint control of the finite block of weighted differences (𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 −𝑔𝑁+1,…,𝑔𝑁+ℎ+𝐿 −𝑔𝑁+𝐿)(gN+h+1−gN+1,…,gN+h+L−gN+L) modulo powers of two, along a block of logarithmic length. We do not know how to obtain such control and we make no progress on it here. The strongest results on prime gaps address a different shape of question. Zhang’s bounded-gap theorem [14] produces infinitely many bounded consecutive-prime gaps. Maynard proves substantially more than an individual-gap statement: [11] bounds lim inf𝑛(𝑝𝑛+𝑚 −𝑝𝑛)lim infn(pn+m−pn) for every fixed 𝑚m, and hence gives bounded clusters of every fixed size; [11] gives the explicit unconditional bound lim inf𝑛(𝑝𝑛+1 −𝑝𝑛) ≤600lim infn(pn+1−pn)≤600. The large-gap theorem of Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard and Tao gives an effective lower bound for the largest single consecutive-prime gap below 𝑋X. None of these results supplies the joint dyadic distribution of a logarithmic block of consecutive gap differences required by eq:truncation. The same introduction notes a separate sequel on chains of large gaps; the cited theorem itself supplies no residue-sensitive block estimate of the kind needed here.

The remaining estimate.

The actual tails satisfy convergence, the prime-to-gap identity, and the recurrence used above. The unresolved input is the joint occurrence in (5.2) for every positive shift. A separate first-moment approach in the companion record uses

∑𝑋≤𝑁<2𝑋𝑇𝑁+𝐿≪𝑋log⁡𝑋(𝐿≤𝑋).∑X≤N<2XTN+L≪Xlog⁡X(L≤X).

It controls the number of excessive omitted tails. A lower bound for the corresponding finite prime-gap configurations is still required. Sparse witness counts can suffice when they exceed that error budget. The independent finite continued-fraction enclosure gives 𝑞 ≥239997 >1012040q≥239997>1012040 for a rational representation of ΠΠ; it makes no assertion about an irrationality exponent.

Statements and declarations

Artefact and data availability.

The source links identify a fixed public snapshot. More recent live declarations are identified explicitly where they are used; a local declaration locator does not establish its presence at a historical public pin. The repository’s versioned source and verification records, rather than this manuscript’s navigation links, identify the checked object. The three finite-computation receipts and their generating programs are public in the computation guide at an immutable revision. That guide records dependencies, replay commands, source provenance, and the exact versus floating-point evidence boundary.

Lean checks each proof term against the fixed library version, and the sources linked here contain no proof placeholders and no project-defined axioms; Lean does not authorise the exposition, the citation choices, or the interpretation, for which the author remains responsible.

For Proposition 1.1, the pair identities, congruence buffer and abstract variable-alphabet filling are checked in SparseRationalisationCore.lean. The explicit three-coordinate schedule, upper Banach density, and block-law transfer are ordinary proofs, given in that proposition and in the companion record, subsection “Paired corrections and cumulative congruences”; they are not Lean- or Comparator-verified. End-to-end sparse candidate sources in the repository are labelled UNRUN and are not presented as checked theorems.

What is checked in Lean
  • The finite summation-by-parts identity relating the prime dyadic partial sums to the prime-gap dyadic partial sums, with an exact endpoint term and no convergence premise.
  • The factor-of-two normalisation between the two displayed indexings, at every finite horizon.
  • Conditional on summability of the prime dyadic series, the exact infinite prime-gap identity and the equivalence of irrationality of the prime and prime-gap series.
  • For an abstract integer-digit dyadic tail recurrence: the exact block identity, and that a shift of fixed length is integral exactly when an explicit scaled state is.
  • That one integral shift propagates to every later index.
  • That repeated doubling removes the power-of-two denominator, so every rational-valued dyadic recurrence has one fixed positive shift integral at all sufficiently late indices.
  • For a real-valued dyadic recurrence, cofinal non-integrality of every fixed positive shift implies irrationality of the initial state.
  • That the actual consecutive-prime-gap sequence is unbounded, by the factorial prime-free-interval construction, and therefore is not eventually periodic with any positive period.
  • For any integer-digit dyadic tail recurrence, two adjacent fixed-length shifts lying strictly between -1 and 1 cannot both be integral when the corresponding digits differ.
  • For the actual prime gaps, a cofinal supply of adjacent small-shift pairs with a mismatching gap excludes eventual integrality of that fixed shift.
  • The generic distance-to-integers core of the finite-truncation criterion: an approximation farther than its error bound from every integer certifies non-integrality.
What is not checked
  • The target irrationality.
  • The definition and recurrence of the concrete prime-gap tail as Lean infinite sums; the note supplies these at paper level. Summability of the concrete prime series is Lean-checked unconditionally via an elementary polynomial prime bound.
  • A theorem supplying cofinally many adjacent actual-prime-gap tail shifts in the open unit interval with the required gap mismatch.
  • Any theorem forcing periodicity or automaticity of the prime gaps from rationality; the free-carry identity disconfirms that route.
The formal record: 5 main results, 3 open obligations, 1 Lean module, Comparator review

Main results

Statements and boundaries are copied from the corpus record. Registry status: not_registered; the claim registry does not carry these declarations and kernel checking them does not promote them into reviewed public claims

formalisation of existing result family: coefficient_only_no_go

The consecutive prime gaps are unbounded.

Unbounded coefficients alone do not force irrationality.

ErdosProblems.Erdos251.exists_primeGap0_gt
formalisation of exact finite identity and nonperiodicity contrast; novelty and significance unassessed family: coefficient_only_no_go

The coefficient-only wrapper records the exact finite carry partial-sum identity together with non-eventual-periodicity of the synthetic coefficient stream and the actual prime-gap stream, exposing the limits of coefficient-only reasoning.

The wrapper proves the finite identity and the two non-eventual-periodicity statements only. It does not assert the infinite rational-sum limit of the synthetic countermodel, identify the synthetic coefficient stream with actual prime gaps, establish a prime-gap tail bridge, prove #251 irrationality, or make novelty, priority, significance, or external-review claims.

ErdosProblems.Erdos251.carryPartialSum_natCast_eq
formalisation of existing result; novelty unassessed family: prime_gap_reformulation

Lean checks that the prime-value dyadic series is irrational exactly when the prime-gap dyadic series is, discharging summability by an elementary polynomial prime bound rather than the prime-number theorem. Neither side is proved irrational. The already-known identity is Tao's (7 October 2025) and is recorded separately as cited only.

The equivalence does not prove irrationality of either series.

ErdosProblems.Erdos251.irrational_tsum_primeDyadicTerm_iff_primeGap
abstract Lean-checked classification and normal form; novelty unassessed family: dyadic_tail_integrality_classification

For any integer-digit real dyadic tail recurrence T(N + 1) = 2*T(N) - g(N + 1), the initial value T(0) is irrational exactly when every positive-length tail shift is nonintegral.

This exact normal form covers arbitrary integer-digit dyadic tail recurrences with the declared real state type; it does not supply a cofinal nonintegral shift for the consecutive-prime-gap recurrence. The prime-specific producer remains open, so no prime-gap irrationality, novelty, significance, or external-review claim is made and Erdős #251 remains open.

ErdosProblems.Erdos251.irrational_initial_iff_all_positive_tailShifts_nonintegral
conditional actual-prime-gap endpoint reduction; novelty and significance unassessed family: small_mismatch_criterion

For the actual prime-gap dyadic tail, cofinally many adjacent pairs of strictly small h-shifts with unequal corresponding prime gaps force failure of eventual RatIntegral h-shifts.

The representative assumes T : ℕ → ℚ, the DyadicTailRecurrence for the actual prime-gap digits, and for every N₀ an 𝑁 ≥N≥ N₀ whose adjacent h-shifts both lie strictly in (-1, 1) while the corresponding prime gaps differ. Under that cofinal small-mismatch supply it excludes eventual RatIntegral h-shifts; it does not prove the supply or actual smallness. rationalPrimeGapTail_has_positive_shift_not_eventually_small records the contrary rational-state obstruction for at least one positive shift. This is a conditional reduction only: no #251 irrationality, infinite rational-sum limit, universal producer, novelty, priority, significance, or external-review claim is made; #251 remains open. The actual-prime-gap specialization is distinct from coefficient_only_no_go and does not duplicate prime_gap_reformulation.

Open obligations

Prove any one of these and the corresponding reduction above becomes unconditional.

  • prime_gap_cofinal_shift_escape For every fixed ℎ ≥1h≥1 and every N0, find N ≥ N0 for which ∑𝑗≥1(𝑔𝑁+ℎ+𝑗 −𝑔𝑁+𝑗)/2𝑗∑j≥1(gN+h+j−gN+j)/2j is not an integer.
  • cofinal_adjacent_small_mismatch For every fixed ℎ ≥1h≥1 and every N0, find N ≥ N0 such that both adjacent full tail shifts have absolute value less than 1 and 𝑔𝑁+ℎ+1 ≠𝑔𝑁+1gN+h+1≠gN+1. The checked local consumer then excludes eventual integrality of the h-shift.
  • actual_prime_gap_tail_formal_bridge Formalise summability of the actual prime and prime-gap dyadic series and identify the concrete infinite prime-gap tail with the checked real/rational dyadic recurrence, so the local consumer reaches the target series without a paper-only analytic bridge.
